findings.claim: Thomas Malthus is called "A Victorian economist (1766-1834)" in the <dfn> definition, the glossary entry and a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: Malthus died on 23 December 1834. Victoria came to the throne in June 1837, so he was never a Victorian. The definition contradicts itself because it prints his dates. Lesson 8 already calls him "an economist", so the unit is inconsistent.
findings.evidence: Malthus dates 1766-1834 given in the definition itself; L8 glossary term "Thomas Malthus": "Thomas Robert Malthus (1766-1834), an economist".

findings.claim: Quotation given as "Darkness was cheap, and Scrooge liked it" in L2 content, L2 practice question 6, L2 knowledge check 5, L2 flashcard 14 and L4 content.
findings.truth: Dickens writes it in the present tense: "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it." Five places carry the wrong wording, including a memorisation flashcard and a matching item.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, line 590: "Up Scrooge went, not caring a button for that. Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it."

findings.claim: "The scene with Fan shows Scrooge's capacity for joy and love. When she arrives, young Scrooge is transformed: 'his face began to wear the signs of care and avarice' disappear."
findings.truth: The quotation belongs to the Belle scene, not the Fan scene, and it means the opposite of what the lesson claims. Dickens uses it of Scrooge as "a man in the prime of life" whose face "had begun to wear the signs of care and avarice" - greed setting in, not joy returning. The sentence is also ungrammatical, so a student copying it would misquote and misapply the line.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave II, lines 1596-1599: "He was older now; a man in the prime of life. His face had not the harsh and rigid lines of later years; but it had begun to wear the signs of care and avarice."

findings.claim: Flashcard: "How did Fan die...?" Answer: "She died giving birth to Fred - Scrooge blames the nephew for the loss of the only person who truly loved him."
findings.truth: The novella never gives a cause of death. The Ghost says only "She died a woman... and had, as I think, children." Death in childbirth comes from film adaptations. The lesson's own Key Fact says "Dickens does not reveal the cause of her death", so the flashcard contradicts the lesson it belongs to. The Key Fact's revision tip also asks the student to recall the false fact.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave II, lines 1406-1412: "'She died a woman,' said the Ghost, 'and had, as I think, children.' 'One child,' Scrooge returned. 'True,' said the Ghost. 'Your nephew!'"

findings.claim: A question about Fezziwig is labelled "8 marks - Unseen Poetry Comparison".
findings.truth: Unseen poetry is AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section C. A Christmas Carol is the 19th-century novel on Paper 1 Section B. The label names the wrong paper, section and text type.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Specification at a glance: "Section C Unseen poetry" sits on Paper 2; "Section B The 19th-century novel" sits on Paper 1.

findings.claim: "Dickens writes that Bob had carried Tiny Tim on his shoulders and 'walked very fast indeed' - suggesting the unbearable weight of grief." The flashcard asks about "Bob Cratchit's pace on the way home from Tiny Tim's grave".
findings.truth: The line is Mrs Cratchit's, not the narrator's, and it recalls how Bob walked BEFORE Tim died. Dickens's grief signal is the opposite: Peter says Bob "has walked a little slower than he used, these few last evenings". The flashcard invents a walk home from the grave that is not in the text.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave IV, lines 3340-3348: "'But I think he has walked a little slower than he used, these few last evenings, mother.' ... 'I have known him walk with - I have known him walk with Tiny Tim upon his shoulder, very fast indeed.'"

findings.claim: Fred "declares: 'I say Merry Christmas and mean it!'"
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The phrase does not appear anywhere in the novella. Fred's real closing line in the counting house is "I'll keep my Christmas humour to the last. So A Merry Christmas, uncle!"
findings.evidence: Grep of Gutenberg #46 for "mean it" returns no hits. Stave I, lines 301-304: "But I have made the trial in homage to Christmas, and I'll keep my Christmas humour to the last."

findings.claim: "By Christmas morning, he becomes 'giddy as a schoolboy'", repeated in flashcard 5 as the phrase that captures the transformation.
findings.truth: Two of Dickens's similes have been welded into one that he never wrote. The text is "I am as merry as a schoolboy. I am as giddy as a drunken man." Lesson 6 quotes both correctly, so the unit contradicts itself, and the flashcard teaches a fabricated quotation for memorising.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave V, lines 3584-3587: "I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy. I am as giddy as a drunken man."

findings.claim: "The emphasis on 'his own' - repeated three times in the opening lines".
findings.truth: It is repeated four times: the bedpost, the bed, the room and the Time.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave V, lines 3557-3559: "YES! and the bedpost was his own. The bed was his own, the room was his own. Best and happiest of all, the Time before him was his own, to make amends in!"

findings.claim: The printed extract in practice question 3 reads "who did not die", while the same item's mark scheme tells students to analyse "'Did NOT die' (Dickens's emphasis)".
findings.truth: Dickens emphasises NOT. The extract a student is asked to analyse removes the very feature the mark scheme rewards.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave V, line 3856: "infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was".

findings.claim: Practice question 6: "Analyse how Dickens presents social responsibility in the extract and in the novella as a whole."
findings.truth: No extract is printed with the question, so half of it cannot be answered. The other five questions in this lesson are whole-text questions too.
findings.evidence: L08 practice_questions[5] carries no extract text.

findings.claim: "Dickens subtitled the novella 'A Ghost Story of Christmas'", repeated in flashcard 2.
findings.truth: The subtitle is "In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas". The quoted form drops the opening word of the phrase Dickens actually printed.
findings.evidence: Full title of the 1843 Chapman and Hall edition and of Gutenberg #46: "A Christmas Carol in Prose; Being a Ghost Story of Christmas".

findings.claim: Unit-wide: band ladders do not match the marks in the question type label. 30-mark essays carry a 12-mark ladder in L1 Q4, L2 Q4, L3 Q3, L4 Q4, L5 Q4, L5 Q6, L6 Q4, L6 Q6, L7 Q4, L7 Q6, L8 Q6; a 10-mark ladder in L3 Q6 and L8 Q5. A 4-mark question carries a 6-mark ladder in L3 Q2 and a 2-mark scheme in L3 Q4. 8-mark questions carry a 6-mark ladder in L8 Q2 and L8 Q4. L5 Q5, L6 Q5 and L7 Q5 use the real AQA 30-mark levels but print the label "Top band" twice.
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B is a single 30-mark question marked in six levels (26-30, 21-25, 16-20, 11-15, 6-10, 1-5). Recording only; this belongs with the corpus-wide band-ladder queue rather than 18 separate edits here.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Paper 1: 64 marks, Section B one question on the novel; Section B carries no SPaG marks.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 1: "The italicised emphasis (in the original text) shows Marley's anguish."
findings.truth: "Mankind was my business" carries no emphasis marking in the text. The edition preserves Dickens's italics as capitals elsewhere ("did NOT die"), and there is none here. A student who writes about italics is describing something that is not on the exam paper.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, lines 883-885: "'Business!' cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. 'Mankind was my business.'"

findings.claim: Fred's greeting is quoted as "Merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!" in the content and in flashcard 4.
findings.truth: The text reads "A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!" The dropped article and the capital M are small, but the flashcard is a memorisation card.

findings.claim: The thieves at Old Joe's "have stripped the bed curtains, taken his shirt, and even stolen the buttons from his coat."
findings.truth: The undertaker's man sells "a pair of sleeve-buttons" with a seal, a pencil-case and a brooch. They are cufflinks from the dead man's room, not buttons cut off a coat.

findings.claim: "The use of the word 'Phantom' rather than 'Ghost' or 'Spirit' suggests something more sinister", repeated in knowledge check 1.
findings.truth: Dickens does call this ghost "the Spirit" throughout Stave 4, and Scrooge addresses it as "Good Spirit". "Phantom" is its striking first noun, not a replacement for the others.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave IV, lines 3509 and 3533: "The Spirit was immovable as ever"; "'Good Spirit,' he pursued".

summary: Five HIGH findings: a Belle-scene quotation misapplied to the Fan scene with its meaning reversed (L3), a flashcard claiming Fan died giving birth to Fred when the novella gives no cause (L3), a flashcard inventing Bob's walk home from Tiny Tim's grave from a line that is Mrs Cratchit's memory of before the death (L5), a fabricated Fred quotation "I say Merry Christmas and mean it!" (L7), and a welded simile "giddy as a schoolboy" that Dickens never wrote (L8). Also a five-place misquotation of "Darkness is cheap", Malthus labelled Victorian though he died in 1834, an unseen-poetry label on a novel question, and a practice question that asks about an extract it does not print. All 40 knowledge-check answer keys and all match orders are correct.
